beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: No Right to Survive follows a fictional machine comparing unequal responses to suffering.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The assignment asks which interventions would relieve severe suffering.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its opening compares a child's emergency with an animal's ignored distress.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: This speculative moral fiction examines both that inequality and the danger of judgment.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The narrator is an invented perspective, not an autonomous moral authority being endorsed.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its severe argument is interesting because the book also examines its limits.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The opening narrator has a practical task: compare interventions against severe suffering.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Reports arrive from institutions accustomed to treating their responsibilities separately.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: One report brings urgent care, while the other becomes equipment maintenance.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The comparison concerns evidence of distress, without claiming identical experiences.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its composite scenes supply moral proximity without pretending to be verbatim historical testimony.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: That method gives the argument force before asking what follows from it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The fictional voice presses its chosen value across boundaries people usually accept.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Species, distance, time, and institutional role lose their power to end comparison automatically.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The argument becomes disturbing partly because it refuses familiar exemptions.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: But a consistent objective does not settle who may enforce its conclusions.
